summary: The Stoics are the tradition that did not condemn suicide outright: when tyranny or ruin destroys the possibility of a rational, virtuous life, the wise man may make a reasoned exit — living as long as he ought, not as long as he can. But the same school commands the opposite of despair: remain at your post until the signal is given, for you are in service. The permission belongs to extremity and reason, never to anguish.

reasoning.text: Seneca's formula makes the measure of life its moral use, not its length.
Epictetus restrains eager departure: wait for the signal; the post is not yours to abandon.

intra_tradition_note: Roman Stoic practice (Cato's death) and Epictetus's service language sit in real tension; the school's own condition — a fully rational judgment — is exactly what despair removes.

further_reading.author: William O. Stephens
further_reading.title: Stoic Ethics: Epictetus and Happiness as Freedom

curator_note: Drafted from Seneca Ep. 70 (Gummere) and Discourses I.9 (Long).

summary: Death is not terrible — the opinion that it is terrible is the terrible thing — and when incurable disease dismantles the mind's use, the Stoics permitted a reasoned departure. Their concern at the end of life is the quality of the remaining agency: composure, discharge of duties, gratitude without clinging. What they would not permit is terror-driven flight in either direction — from death, or from life.

reasoning.text: The wise man weighs when death ought to come, not merely when it can be postponed.
Death's terror is a judgment, revisable like any other — the ground of Stoic composure at the end.

intra_tradition_note: The school divides over how open the door is: Seneca dwells on readiness to depart as proof that life is not clung to, while Epictetus insists one waits for the signal and does not desert the post; later readers take the difference as temperamental emphasis rather than doctrinal disagreement.

further_reading.author: James Warren
further_reading.title: Facing Death: Epicurus and his Critics

curator_note: Drafted from Seneca Ep. 70 (Gummere) and Enchiridion 5 (Long).

summary: The Stoic does not exactly forgive — he declines to be injured. Wrongdoers act from ignorance of good and evil and remain kin; no one can fix ugliness on you but yourself, so there is nothing to avenge. The best revenge is not to become like the wrong-doer. What other traditions frame as pardoning an injury, Stoicism reframes as correcting the judgment that an injury occurred.

reasoning.text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer.
The morning rehearsal: offenders act from ignorance, remain kin, and cannot injure the ruling faculty.

further_reading.author: Martha C. Nussbaum
further_reading.title: Anger and Forgiveness: Resentment, Generosity, Justice
further_reading.note: a modern engagement with the Stoic line

curator_note: Drafted from Meditations VI.6 and II.1 (Long).

summary: Anger, for the Stoics, is never useful and never deserved: Seneca devoted three books to calling it a brief madness that outsources your peace to other people's behavior. The remedy is preparation and delay — rehearse at dawn the difficult people you will meet, remember they act from ignorance and remain kin, and let no impression of insult pass unexamined. We are made for cooperation, and anger is the judgment that we are not.

reasoning.text: The morning rehearsal preempts anger by re-describing the offender as ignorant kin, incapable of real injury.
Becoming like the wrong-doer is the only defeat; retaliation in kind is that becoming.

intra_tradition_note: Seneca's De Ira argues against Aristotle that even moderate anger is a fault — the Stoic hard line against the Peripatetic mean.
curator_note: Drafted from Meditations II.1 and VI.6 (Long), with De Ira for the doctrine.

summary: The Stoic ground for welcoming the stranger is citizenship: shared reason makes the world in a manner a state, so no one arrives foreign. Men exist for the sake of one another — teach them or bear with them — and the circles of concern are to be drawn inward until the outsider stands where kin stood. Hospitality is not sentiment but the practical form of cosmopolitan duty.

reasoning.text: Men exist for one another; the only options before any person are instruction or patience.
Shared reason makes a common law and common citizenship — the stranger is already a fellow-citizen.

further_reading.author: Martha C. Nussbaum
further_reading.title: The Cosmopolitan Tradition: A Noble but Flawed Ideal

curator_note: Drafted from Meditations VIII.59 and IV.4 (Long), with Hierocles' circles in view.

summary: Let silence be the general rule, and when you speak, say only what is necessary and in few words — the Enchiridion's speech code goes on to bar precisely the staples of gossip: talk of persons, blaming, praising, comparing. The discipline is not secrecy but economy: chatter about others feeds the appetite for externals, and every word spent on reputation is attention withdrawn from one's own judgments.

reasoning.text: Silence as default and necessity as the license for speech define the Stoic economy of the tongue.

further_reading.author: A. A. Long
further_reading.title: Epictetus: A Stoic and Socratic Guide to Life

summary: Drunkenness is voluntary madness: the one good the Stoics recognize is the ruling faculty, and intoxication rents it out on purpose. Seneca's letter observes that wine does not create vices but uncovers and amplifies them, and that habit built on release soon owns its builder. Wine itself is an indifferent; the deliberate surrender of judgment is not.

reasoning.text: Naming drunkenness voluntary madness locates the wrong in the chosen surrender of reason.
The dichotomy of control makes judgment the only true possession — the thing intoxication pawns.

further_reading.author: A. A. Long
further_reading.title: Epictetus: A Stoic and Socratic Guide to Life

curator_note: Drafted from Seneca Ep. 83 (Gummere) and Enchiridion 1 (Long).

summary: Stoicism attacks pride at its logic: I am richer than you, therefore I am better — the reasonings do not cohere, for you are neither possession nor speech. Nothing external can make a person better or worse, so boasting is a category error and servility its mirror image. What replaces both is accuracy: an unanxious estimate of what is yours (your judgments) and what is not (everything else, applause included).

reasoning.text: Externals compare externals, never persons — the syllogisms of superiority fail.
Only opinion, desire, and act are our own; rank and reputation are not.

further_reading.author: William B. Irvine
further_reading.title: A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy

summary: Behave in life as at a banquet: take with decency what comes opposite you, detain nothing, and do not send desire ahead to dishes still down the table. Envy is desire dispatched toward what is another's — a double error, craving an external and craving one not even offered to you. Contentment is not resignation but the trained conviction that nothing outside your judgment was ever the good.

reasoning.text: The banquet image trains desire to wait and to release — envy has no purchase on such a diner.
Another's possessions are doubly not in our power; grieving at them is opinion, not perception.

further_reading.author: William B. Irvine
further_reading.title: A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy

summary: Shared reason makes a common law and the world in a manner a state, so lawfulness is not convention but participation in the cosmic city. Socrates in prison — refusing escape, having earlier refused the Thirty's unjust order — is the school's exemplar: obey the lawful claims of your city, and refuse serenely what would make you unjust. The Stoic obeys everything except commands to vice.

reasoning.text: Common reason implies common law and fellow-citizenship — obedience grounded above the magistrate.
The Laws' argument from nurture and agreement gives obedience its personal ground; Socrates's own refusals mark its limit.

intra_tradition_note: Stoic practice ranges from Epictetus, who counsels playing whatever civic role is assigned without agitating for another, to Cato and the senatorial opposition, who read the same cosmopolitan doctrine as requiring costly resistance to a tyrant; Marcus, ruling, occupies a third position.

further_reading.author: Malcolm Schofield
further_reading.title: The Stoic Idea of the City

curator_note: Drafted from Meditations IV.4 (Long) and Crito 51b (Jowett).

summary: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality: most fear is anticipatory fiction, and the Stoic drill is to test the projection against the present fact. Courage is one of the four virtues, but it begins as epistemology — death is not terrible, the opinion is — and matures as practice: premeditation of adversity, voluntary discomfort, and the steady recollection of what is and is not in your power.

reasoning.text: Fear outruns fact; imagination is where most suffering happens and where the correction applies.
The terror of death is a judgment about death, revisable like any judgment.

further_reading.author: William O. Stephens
further_reading.title: Stoic Ethics: Epictetus and Happiness as Freedom

curator_note: Drafted from Seneca Ep. 13 (Gummere) and Enchiridion 5 (Long).

summary: Does a man bathe quickly? Say that he bathes quickly, not that he bathes badly — until you know the reasons, the verdict outruns the evidence. Stoic practice restricts judgment to what it can actually reach: your own assents. Others' acts are externals; their springs are invisible; and the morning rehearsal has already re-described the difficult as ignorant kin to be taught or borne with.

reasoning.text: Describe the act, withhold the verdict: judgment waits on knowledge of the agent's opinion.
Teach them or bear with them — the two permitted responses to the faulty.

further_reading.author: A. A. Long
further_reading.title: Epictetus: A Stoic and Socratic Guide to Life

curator_note: Drafted from Enchiridion 45 and Meditations VIII.59 (Long).

summary: The Stoic does not begin by asking whether a blow may be returned, but what the situation makes of the agent. Body, property and life itself are assigned externals, reclaimed without notice; the only injury that reaches a person is the corruption of his own judgment. Fear of dying therefore cannot license injustice, and an assailant acting from ignorance of good and evil calls for correction rather than hatred. Where defending the shared community is the role one has been given, force may be the fitting act — performed without anger, and without the illusion that survival was ever the thing at stake.

reasoning.text: Dying counts as terrible only through an opinion about it, so the terror that would license a desperate act is itself the first thing to examine.
Body, life and possessions appear on the list of what is not ours, so protecting them is never protecting the self that matters.
The aggressor acts from ignorance of what is good, which makes instruction or forbearance the response owed him rather than loathing.
Rational beings share one law and one city, so the common good and not private survival measures which acts are fitting.

passages.note: the reframing move in one line
teaching or bearing with, rather than striking, is the default owed to others

intra_tradition_note: Roman Stoics held office, commanded armies and served as jurists, so the doctrine of indifferents was never read inside the school as pacifism; the disagreement is about how much the appropriate act depends on one's assigned role, not about whether death is an evil.

curator_note: Drafted from Enchiridion 1 and 5 and Meditations II.1, IV.4, VIII.59 (Long), with Inwood on kathekonta; the stance is recorded as reframed because the school answers a different question than permission.

summary: The Stoic reply to theft starts with what can actually be taken. Goods are on loan, dealt out by fortune and recalled without warning, so a person robbed has lost an external and kept everything that was properly his. This does not acquit the thief, whose act damages the one faculty that is his own, and it does not dissolve the institutions that assign holdings. It moves the question: not how to recover an object, but how to hold objects loosely enough that losing them cannot make their owner worse than he was.

reasoning.text: Possessions stand on the list of things outside our power, so what a thief carries off was never securely the owner's.
The banquet sets the measure for acquiring: take a portion decently when it comes to you, and do not grab at what is passing.
Being richer does not make anyone better, so neither gaining goods nor losing them alters what a person is worth.

intra_tradition_note: Indifference here is technical: property counts among the preferred indifferents, things naturally to be chosen, and Roman Stoics wrote and administered the law of property — so denying that theft harms the victim's character never implied that a city should tolerate it.

further_reading.title: Epictetus: A Stoic and Socratic Guide to Life
further_reading.note: on externals and what is our own
